editorNote: IBM puts its standard-setting PC architecture into a 30-pound suitcase while Sinclair aims a far cheaper QL at American home offices and three corporate giants place a bet on videotex.
morningLine: The computer road warrior now has an IBM badge, an amber screen and a very sturdy carrying arm.

lead.headline: IBM Packs the PC into a 30-Pound Suitcase
lead.dek: The $4,225 Portable Personal Computer answers Compaq with PC/XT compatibility, twin floppy drives and a built-in amber screen.
body: IBM entered the suitcase-computer contest on February 16 with the Portable Personal Computer model 5155, putting the familiar IBM PC architecture into a transportable case. Contemporary coverage made the competitive target plain: Compaq had proved that business buyers wanted a machine they could carry between offices without leaving their software behind.

Inside, the new portable followed the PC/XT line with a 4.77 MHz Intel 8088 processor and 256 KB of memory, expandable to 640 KB. Two 360 KB 5.25-inch floppy drives sat beside a built-in 9-inch amber display, while the detachable keyboard clipped across the front for travel.

Portable remained a relative term. The 5155 weighed about 30 pounds, required AC power and cost $4,225. It was a luggable business computer rather than a battery-powered laptop, aimed at professionals who valued IBM compatibility enough to carry the weight and pay the premium.

That compatibility may be the machine’s strongest feature. Buyers could take established IBM PC programs and disks on the road, and corporate departments could add a mobile system without adopting a separate software standard. The 5155 shows how quickly the compatible-PC market is forcing IBM to answer categories created by its rivals.

stories.headline: Sinclair Sets a $499 American Course for the QL
body: Sinclair Research said on February 13 that it planned to bring the QL to American consumers in the fall for $499. The Quantum Leap uses a Motorola 68008 processor, carries 128 KB of memory and aims above Sinclair’s inexpensive ZX home machines at home-office and small-business users.

Its value pitch is unusually ambitious: two built-in Microdrives, a professional keyboard, color-display capability and a bundled Psion suite covering word processing, spreadsheets, databases and business graphics. The promised price puts pressure on machines costing several times more, though American buyers must wait to see whether Sinclair meets its delivery plans.

stories.headline: CBS, IBM and Sears Bet on a Videotex Home
body: CBS, IBM and Sears joined forces in the electronic information-services field this week, combining a broadcaster, the dominant computer maker and a retail giant in a bid to reach consumers by telephone line. The alliance intensifies the race to turn home terminals into gateways for news, shopping, banking and communications.

The venture reflects a sweeping expectation that networked information will become a household business. Modems remain slow and the audience small, but the partners bring content, technical reach and retail familiarity to a market still searching for the service that will persuade families to go online.

stories.headline: Coleco Courts Publishers for Adam “Best Of” Albums
body: A tightly dated Electronic Games Hotline report says Coleco plans “best of” software albums for the Adam, seeking deals with established publishers to strengthen the computer’s thin catalog. The move follows a difficult holiday introduction marked by questions about reliability and performance.

Compilations could give Adam owners recognizable games while helping Coleco show that its computer has a future beyond bundled software. For now the report describes a publishing plan, not finished albums on store shelves; execution will matter as much as the names Coleco signs.
